title: The linear life cycle
blurb: Name the four linear phases in order and say exactly what happens in Concept, Definition, Deployment and Transition.
question: A school extension project has just had its detailed plans, schedule and budget approved, and the contractor is about to start on site. Which phase has just finished, which phase is starting, and which phase will come last?

teach.body: A linear life cycle is a sequential life cycle: its phases follow one after another, and each phase is largely completed before the next begins. The four phases, in order, are Concept, Definition, Deployment and Transition. In plain English: decide whether it's worth doing, plan it properly, build it, then hand it over. It suits projects whose requirements are stable and well understood from the start.

teach.caption: Memory hook: 'Can Dave Deliver Tomorrow?' Definition (plan) always comes before Deployment (build).

teach.h: Definition sets the baseline for the whole project
teach.body: By the end of Definition, the project has detailed requirements and a project management plan, and the deployment baseline is set for the WHOLE project: scope, schedule, cost, resources and quality. Scope is fixed, and any change after that goes through formal change control. Deployment progress is then measured against this baseline. That is the heart of a linear approach: plan fully, then deliver to the plan.

Concept: the school needs two more classrooms, so an outline business case checks the need, options and rough cost. Definition: an architect produces the design, requirements are agreed, a contractor is chosen and the plan and baseline are approved. Deployment: the contractor builds and tests the extension while progress is tracked. Transition: the school accepts the building, the team is released, the project closes and lessons are captured.

teach.h: When linear fits, and when it doesn't

teach.text: Order trap: Definition (plan) comes BEFORE Deployment (build), and Transition, not Deployment, is the LAST phase. Name trap: older material (BoK 6th edition) used Concept, Definition, Implementation, Handover and closure, and some sources say 'Development'. For the PFQ, use Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition.

items: Linear phases in order: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition.
Each phase is largely completed before the next; gates sit between them.
Concept: idea, outline business case, strategic fit, feasibility.
Definition: requirements, PMP, deployment baseline for the whole project.
Deployment: build, test, deliver, monitor and control. Transition: handover, acceptance, closure, lessons.

summary: You can now state the four phases of a linear life cycle in order and describe what happens in each one. You can also spot a phase from its activities and explain why Definition sets a whole-project baseline.

A.q: In a linear life cycle, which phase comes immediately after Definition?
A.why: The linear order is Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition, so Deployment follows Definition.

whyNot.0: Transition is the last phase; it follows Deployment.
whyNot.2: Concept is the first phase, before Definition.
whyNot.3: Foundations is an iterative phase name, not a linear one.

A.q: In which linear phase is the idea first developed, with an outline business case and a check of strategic fit?
A.why: Concept develops the idea or need, produces an outline business case and checks strategic fit and feasibility.

whyNot.0: Definition refines the business case and produces detailed plans; the idea already exists by then.
whyNot.1: Deployment is where the outputs are built.
whyNot.2: Transition hands the outputs over and closes the project.

A.q: A contractor is on site building new classrooms, and progress is checked against the approved plan. Which linear phase is this?
A.why: Deployment is where the work is done: outputs are built, tested and delivered while progress is monitored and controlled.

whyNot.1: Definition produces the plan that Deployment works to.
whyNot.2: Concept is about the idea and outline business case, long before building starts.
whyNot.3: Transition follows the build, when the outputs are handed over.

B.q: Which is the FINAL phase of a typical linear project life cycle?
B.why: Transition is the last linear phase: outputs are handed over, resources released and the project closed.

whyNot.1: Closure happens within Transition; it isn't the name of a linear phase.
whyNot.3: Adoption is added by the extended life cycle, after Transition.

B.q: In a linear life cycle, at the end of which phase is the deployment baseline set for the whole project?
B.why: Definition produces the detailed plans, and the deployment baseline for the whole project is set at its end.

whyNot.0: Concept only has an outline business case; there isn't enough detail for a baseline.
whyNot.2: Deployment is measured against the baseline, so it must already exist.
whyNot.3: By Transition the work is complete; a baseline is no longer being set.

B.q: Which activity belongs in the Transition phase of a linear life cycle?
B.why: Transition hands the outputs to users and BAU, gains acceptance, releases resources and closes the project with lessons learned.

whyNot.0: Strategic fit is checked in Concept.
whyNot.1: Detailed requirements are agreed in Definition.
whyNot.2: Building and testing happen in Deployment.

C.q: Complete the sequence of a linear life cycle: Concept, ___, Deployment, Transition.
C.why: The second linear phase is Definition: the plan is made before the build starts.

whyNot.0: 'Development' is not a BoK 7 linear phase name; it echoes the iterative 'Evolutionary development'.
whyNot.1: Foundations is the second phase of the ITERATIVE life cycle.
whyNot.3: Feasibility is the first phase of the ITERATIVE life cycle.

C.q: A new HR system has passed its tests. Users are being trained, the business is formally accepting it and the project team is being released. Which phase is this?
C.why: Handover to users, acceptance and releasing the team are all Transition activities.

whyNot.1: Deployment built and tested the system; that work is now finished.
whyNot.2: Definition was the planning phase before the build.
whyNot.3: Benefits realisation is an extra phase in the extended life cycle, after Adoption.

C.q:
Which TWO statements about a linear life cycle are correct?
1) Each phase is largely completed before the next
2) Scope flexes in every time box
3) It suits stable, well-understood requirements
4) Its first phase is Feasibility
C.why: A linear life cycle is sequential and suits stable requirements.

whyNot.0: Scope flexing within time boxes describes an iterative life cycle.
whyNot.1: Both describe the iterative life cycle, not the linear one.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is right, but the linear life cycle starts with Concept, not Feasibility.

reteach.title: Planning a wedding, the linear way
reteach.question: A couple plan their wedding: they decide whether to marry and roughly what it will cost, book everything, hold the big day, then return the hired suits and thank the guests. Which linear phase is each step?

blocks.body: Concept: 'Shall we get married, and can we afford it?' Definition: the guest list, venue, budget and timetable are agreed and booked. Deployment: the big day itself, run to that plan. Transition: hired items returned, suppliers paid, thank-you cards sent, and the couple start married life. You wouldn't hold the day before booking the venue: that's why Definition comes before Deployment.

blocks.h: The wedding as a linear life cycle

blocks.text: The day itself is Deployment, not the end. The wrap-up afterwards is Transition, the final phase.

explain.body: The first phase. Develop the idea or need, produce an outline business case, and check strategic fit and feasibility. The gate at the end decides whether the idea is worth planning in detail.

test.q: Which question is the Concept phase mainly trying to answer?
test.why: Concept tests whether the idea is worth pursuing, using an outline business case and a check of strategic fit and feasibility.

whyNot.1: Schedule performance is tracked in Deployment.
whyNot.2: Releasing the team happens in Transition.
whyNot.3: Acceptance of outputs happens in Transition.

explain.body: Define the requirements and how the work will be done. Detailed plans are written in the project management plan, the business case is refined, and the deployment baseline is set for the whole project.

items.label: how the project will be delivered

test.q: Which document is typically produced in Definition to set out how the project will be delivered?
test.why: The project management plan (PMP) is produced in Definition and documents how the project will be delivered.

whyNot.0: Lessons learned are captured at closure in Transition.
whyNot.2: Benefits reviews take place after handover.
whyNot.3: Acceptance of outputs happens in Transition.

explain.body: Do the work: build, test and deliver the outputs. The project manager monitors and controls progress against the deployment baseline, and changes go through change control.

test.q: During Deployment in a linear life cycle, what is progress measured against?
test.why: Deployment progress is measured and controlled against the deployment baseline set at the end of Definition.

whyNot.0: The outline business case comes from Concept and is too high level to measure delivery progress.
whyNot.1: Benefits are reviewed after handover, not used to track the build.
whyNot.3: Lessons are captured at closure; they aren't a progress yardstick.

explain.body: The last phase. Outputs are handed over to users and business as usual, accepted, resources are released, the project is formally closed and lessons learned are captured.

test.q: Which of these happens in the Transition phase?
options: The outline business case is written
The outputs are built and tested
The outputs are handed over to users
test.why: Transition hands the outputs over to users and BAU, then closes the project.

whyNot.0: The outline business case is a Concept output.
whyNot.1: Detailed requirements are agreed in Definition.
whyNot.2: Building and testing happen in Deployment.
